Reading the Dust Bowl: Vernacular Photography and Agricultural Memory in Western
Oklahoma, 1930-1945

by

Cortez, Daniel R.

A thesis submitted in partial fulfillment
of the requirements for the degree of
Master of Arts
Department of History
2021

Thesis Committee:

Dr. Ingrid Solberg, Committee Chair
Professor Nathaniel Ozawa
Dr. Fatima El-Sayed

ABSTRACT  Between 1930 and 1945 farming families in five western Oklahoma counties
produced thousands of snapshots that circulated privately for decades before entering
public archives. This thesis reads 412 such photographs alongside oral histories and
county extension records to argue that vernacular photography preserved an
agricultural memory markedly different from the one built by federal documentary
projects of the same period. Where Farm Security Administration images emphasised
displacement and ruin, family photographs foreground continuity: machinery
maintenance, harvest gatherings, and church picnics recur far more often than dust or
abandonment. Reading these collections as deliberate acts of record-keeping rather
than incidental snapshots recovers a rural self-representation that complicates the
regional narrative inherited from documentary photography, and suggests that
archival appraisal practices have themselves shaped what the Dust Bowl is remembered
to have been.
